commit_message:
Update release process (#25002)

* pypi_deploy.sh: dry run by default (`twine check`), `--publish` to
upload. `--wheel-dir` publishes the wheels of a previous dry run without
downloading them again. Missing packages need confirmation.
* Add a release tracker template
* release-management.md: document the missing tracker steps
* RELEASING.md: fix the iree-turbine release docs link.

Co-Authored-By: Claude

commit_message:
[Torch] Convert PT2E per-token quantization to LinalgExt

Convert quantized_decomposed.quantize_per_token and dequantize_per_token
to iree_linalg_ext.quantize_affine and dequantize_affine. As in torchao's
PerToken granularity, the block size is one along every input dimension
but the last, which each block spans, so the parameters are indexed by
the leading dimensions and the data path needs no reshape. The unit last
dimension that PT2E keeps in the parameters is dropped like any other
static unit dimension.

Per-token shares its operand checks with per-channel-group, which expect
one scale and zero point per block along each input dimension.

Quantize scales are widened as for the other granularities, so
quantization computes in the wider of the input and scale types, as the
per-token reference does, but in at least f32. Dequantization matches
the PT2E reference. The per-token reference adds the zero point before
rounding, so quantize ties with odd zero points differ from it and from
the Torch-to-Linalg lowering, which follows it.

Depends on the torch-mlir ops from llvm/torch-mlir#4765.

Signed-off-by: Roberto Laudani <laudani@roofline.ai>
name: setup / setup

commit_message:
[Torch] Convert PT2E per-token quantization to LinalgExt

Convert quantized_decomposed.quantize_per_token and dequantize_per_token
to iree_linalg_ext.quantize_affine and dequantize_affine. As in torchao's
PerToken granularity, the block size is one along every input dimension
but the last, which each block spans, so the parameters are indexed by
the leading dimensions and the data path needs no reshape. The unit last
dimension that PT2E keeps in the parameters is dropped like any other
static unit dimension.

Per-token shares its operand checks with per-channel-group, which expect
one scale and zero point per block along each input dimension.

Quantize scales are widened as for the other granularities, so
quantization computes in the wider of the input and scale types, as the
per-token reference does, but in at least f32. Dequantization matches
the PT2E reference. The per-token reference adds the zero point before
rounding, so quantize ties with odd zero points differ from it and from
the Torch-to-Linalg lowering, which follows it.

Depends on the torch-mlir ops from llvm/torch-mlir#4765.

Signed-off-by: Roberto Laudani <laudani@roofline.ai>

commit_message:
[Torch] Convert PT2E per-token quantization to LinalgExt

Convert quantized_decomposed.quantize_per_token and dequantize_per_token
to iree_linalg_ext.quantize_affine and dequantize_affine. As in torchao's
PerToken granularity, the block size is one along every input dimension
but the last, which each block spans, so the parameters are indexed by
the leading dimensions and the data path needs no reshape. The unit last
dimension that PT2E keeps in the parameters is dropped like any other
static unit dimension.

Per-token shares its operand checks with per-channel-group, which expect
one scale and zero point per block along each input dimension.

Quantize scales are widened as for the other granularities, so
quantization computes in the wider of the input and scale types, as the
per-token reference does, but in at least f32. Dequantization matches
the PT2E reference. The per-token reference adds the zero point before
rounding, so quantize ties with odd zero points differ from it and from
the Torch-to-Linalg lowering, which follows it.

Depends on the torch-mlir ops from llvm/torch-mlir#4765.

commit_message:
[Torch] Convert PT2E per-token quantization to LinalgExt

Convert quantized_decomposed.quantize_per_token and dequantize_per_token
to iree_linalg_ext.quantize_affine and dequantize_affine. As in torchao's
PerToken granularity, the block size is one along every input dimension
but the last, which each block spans, so the parameters are indexed by
the leading dimensions and the data path needs no reshape. The unit last
dimension that PT2E keeps in the parameters is dropped like any other
static unit dimension.

Per-token shares its operand checks with per-channel-group, which expect
one scale and zero point per block along each input dimension.

Quantize scales are widened as for the other granularities, so
quantization computes in the wider of the input and scale types, as the
per-token reference does, but in at least f32. Dequantization matches
the PT2E reference. The per-token reference adds the zero point before
rounding, so quantize ties with odd zero points differ from it and from
the Torch-to-Linalg lowering, which follows it.

Depends on the torch-mlir ops from llvm/torch-mlir#4765.

Signed-off-by: Roberto Laudani <laudani@roofline.ai>
name: clang-tidy

dequantize_per_channel_group to iree_linalg_ext.quantize_affine and
dequantize_affine, so later QDQ optimizations see the groups instead of
the floordiv-indexed arithmetic of Torch-to-Linalg.

torchao-style block size. LinalgExt parameter maps must be projected
permutations, so a dimension with several blocks of several elements is
split into the block and the position within it, and the result is
collapsed back. The scale and zero point are indexed without their
static unit dimensions, which also applies to per-channel quantization
along an axis of size one.

scales.

overflows when subtracting the zero point in the storage type. The
reference quantizes by adding the zero point before rounding, so ties
with odd zero points differ, as they already do in Torch-to-Linalg.

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Fold empty-set reductions to their init operand. (#24949)

Reductions over a zero-sized dimension (e.g. input shape 2x0x4 -> 2x1x4)
lower to a linalg.generic with a 0-extent input, which crashes codegen
tiling (computeAllSliceParameters assertion).
    
When the reduced dimension has size 0, no input element is ever
combined,
so the result of the reduction is exactly its init operand. This adds a
pattern in RemoveZeroExtentTensors that replaces such a reduction with
its
existing init operand, so the 0-extent generic never reaches codegen.
    
Forwarding the init (instead of synthesizing a linalg.fill of the
reduction
identity) preserves the semantics of any initial accumulator value,
including
non-identity ones, and avoids materializing a new fill. For ONNX
empty-set
reductions the init already carries the identity (sum -> 0, prod -> 1),
so the observable result is unchanged.

Adds lit coverage for the rewrite:
  - a reduction with a non-identity initial accumulator (init preserved),
  - dynamic output dimensions.
    
Fixes 8 onnx_ops *_empty_set cases:
    test_reduce_sum_empty_set
    test_reduce_sum_square_empty_set
    test_reduce_sum_square_empty_set_expanded
    test_reduce_l1_empty_set
    test_reduce_l1_empty_set_expanded
    test_reduce_l2_empty_set
    test_reduce_log_sum_empty_set
    test_reduce_log_sum_exp_empty_set
    
Related to iree-org/iree#24378

commit_message:
[Stream] Always map aliases to resolved resource ranges of the source op (#25026)

This ensures that all operands in the tied operand chain for a resource
will get mapped to the correct buffer range.

Previously, if the resource's buffer received a new allocation,
`stream.resource.subview` aliases (by nature of a byte subview, tied to
a different memory range) would still receive resource ranges relatively
to the old resource.
Additionally, all aliases of a given source would be processed from the
"nearest" subview in the alias chain. With multiple subviews in the same
tied operand chain, the offsets weren't computed relative to one
another.

Addressing the first problem enables the most practical use case.
SplitParameterEncoding in "consolidate" mode may need to place an
unmodified input weight into the output buffers, which means the weight
may end up in a packed allocation together with a pre-initialized output
parameter. To later fetch that input weight for dynamic initialization,
an explicit `subview` op is generated (*). Hoisting the constant out of
the execution scope establishes the new resource range, and the subview
should compute its resource range against that. Instead, the old
subrange would get used that was relative to the original SSA source
bound for deletion.
See `Stream/Transforms/test/schedule_allocation_subviews_constant.mlir`
for illustration.

(*) Whether that should be happening is a different matter. Accessing
the packed weight through `stream.async.slice` would've been preferable,
as per a [TODO in
SplitParameterEncoder](https://github.com/iree-org/iree/blob/0df50f9a8e40ab1878479124b952f45d9f8c0650/compiler/src/iree/compiler/Dialect/Stream/Transforms/SplitParameterEncoder.cpp#L1971).
Generally, we should let ScheduleAllocation operate on that abstraction
where a copy will implicitly be generated on writing to the range,
rather than have it account for explicit aliases in that of
`resource.subview`. For now I've preferred not to go into that
direction, because that switch requires larger-scale testing, and
currently explicit subview ops are expected to be supported in the input
IR to the allocator.

By implementing alias mapping as a DFS worklist and simply ignoring
values that have already been resolved to a resource range, nested
subviews, a.k.a. subview ops that reference each other, now correctly
calculate their offset by adding up their own offset to the earlier
offsets in the tied operand chain. Not sure if that does/would come up
in a real case, but at least that's a sensible side effect.

commit_message:
[Stream] Always map aliases to resolved resource ranges of the source op (#25026)

This ensures that all operands in the tied operand chain for a resource
will get mapped to the correct buffer range.

Previously, if the resource's buffer received a new allocation,
`stream.resource.subview` aliases (by nature of a byte subview, tied to
a different memory range) would still receive resource ranges relatively
to the old resource.
Additionally, all aliases of a given source would be processed from the
"nearest" subview in the alias chain. With multiple subviews in the same
tied operand chain, the offsets weren't computed relative to one
another.

Addressing the first problem enables the most practical use case.
SplitParameterEncoding in "consolidate" mode may need to place an
unmodified input weight into the output buffers, which means the weight
may end up in a packed allocation together with a pre-initialized output
parameter. To later fetch that input weight for dynamic initialization,
an explicit `subview` op is generated (*). Hoisting the constant out of
the execution scope establishes the new resource range, and the subview
should compute its resource range against that. Instead, the old
subrange would get used that was relative to the original SSA source
bound for deletion.
See `Stream/Transforms/test/schedule_allocation_subviews_constant.mlir`
for illustration.

(*) Whether that should be happening is a different matter. Accessing
the packed weight through `stream.async.slice` would've been preferable,
as per a [TODO in
SplitParameterEncoder](https://github.com/iree-org/iree/blob/0df50f9a8e40ab1878479124b952f45d9f8c0650/compiler/src/iree/compiler/Dialect/Stream/Transforms/SplitParameterEncoder.cpp#L1971).
Generally, we should let ScheduleAllocation operate on that abstraction
where a copy will implicitly be generated on writing to the range,
rather than have it account for explicit aliases in that of
`resource.subview`. For now I've preferred not to go into that
direction, because that switch requires larger-scale testing, and
currently explicit subview ops are expected to be supported in the input
IR to the allocator.

By implementing alias mapping as a DFS worklist and simply ignoring
values that have already been resolved to a resource range, nested
subviews, a.k.a. subview ops that reference each other, now correctly
calculate their offset by adding up their own offset to the earlier
offsets in the tied operand chain. Not sure if that does/would come up
in a real case, but at least that's a sensible side effect.

commit_message:
[Stream] Always map aliases to resolved resource ranges of the source op (#25026)

This ensures that all operands in the tied operand chain for a resource
will get mapped to the correct buffer range.

Previously, if the resource's buffer received a new allocation,
`stream.resource.subview` aliases (by nature of a byte subview, tied to
a different memory range) would still receive resource ranges relatively
to the old resource.
Additionally, all aliases of a given source would be processed from the
"nearest" subview in the alias chain. With multiple subviews in the same
tied operand chain, the offsets weren't computed relative to one
another.

Addressing the first problem enables the most practical use case.
SplitParameterEncoding in "consolidate" mode may need to place an
unmodified input weight into the output buffers, which means the weight
may end up in a packed allocation together with a pre-initialized output
parameter. To later fetch that input weight for dynamic initialization,
an explicit `subview` op is generated (*). Hoisting the constant out of
the execution scope establishes the new resource range, and the subview
should compute its resource range against that. Instead, the old
subrange would get used that was relative to the original SSA source
bound for deletion.
See `Stream/Transforms/test/schedule_allocation_subviews_constant.mlir`
for illustration.

(*) Whether that should be happening is a different matter. Accessing
the packed weight through `stream.async.slice` would've been preferable,
as per a [TODO in
SplitParameterEncoder](https://github.com/iree-org/iree/blob/0df50f9a8e40ab1878479124b952f45d9f8c0650/compiler/src/iree/compiler/Dialect/Stream/Transforms/SplitParameterEncoder.cpp#L1971).
Generally, we should let ScheduleAllocation operate on that abstraction
where a copy will implicitly be generated on writing to the range,
rather than have it account for explicit aliases in that of
`resource.subview`. For now I've preferred not to go into that
direction, because that switch requires larger-scale testing, and
currently explicit subview ops are expected to be supported in the input
IR to the allocator.

By implementing alias mapping as a DFS worklist and simply ignoring
values that have already been resolved to a resource range, nested
subviews, a.k.a. subview ops that reference each other, now correctly
calculate their offset by adding up their own offset to the earlier
offsets in the tied operand chain. Not sure if that does/would come up
in a real case, but at least that's a sensible side effect.

This ensures that all operands in the tied operand chain for a resource
will get mapped to the correct buffer range.

Previously, if the resource's buffer received a new allocation,
`stream.resource.subview` aliases (by nature of a byte subview, tied to
a different memory range) would still receive resource ranges relatively
to the old resource.
Additionally, all aliases of a given source would be processed from the
"nearest" subview in the alias chain. With multiple subviews in the same
tied operand chain, the offsets weren't computed relative to one
another.

Addressing the first problem enables the most practical use case.
SplitParameterEncoding in "consolidate" mode may need to place an
unmodified input weight into the output buffers, which means the weight
may end up in a packed allocation together with a pre-initialized output
parameter. To later fetch that input weight for dynamic initialization,
an explicit `subview` op is generated (*). Hoisting the constant out of
the execution scope establishes the new resource range, and the subview
should compute its resource range against that. Instead, the old
subrange would get used that was relative to the original SSA source
bound for deletion.
See `Stream/Transforms/test/schedule_allocation_subviews_constant.mlir`
for illustration.

(*) Whether that should be happening is a different matter. Accessing
the packed weight through `stream.async.slice` would've been preferable,
as per a [TODO in
SplitParameterEncoder](https://github.com/iree-org/iree/blob/0df50f9a8e40ab1878479124b952f45d9f8c0650/compiler/src/iree/compiler/Dialect/Stream/Transforms/SplitParameterEncoder.cpp#L1971).
Generally, we should let ScheduleAllocation operate on that abstraction
where a copy will implicitly be generated on writing to the range,
rather than have it account for explicit aliases in that of
`resource.subview`. For now I've preferred not to go into that
direction, because that switch requires larger-scale testing, and
currently explicit subview ops are expected to be supported in the input
IR to the allocator.

By implementing alias mapping as a DFS worklist and simply ignoring
values that have already been resolved to a resource range, nested
subviews, a.k.a. subview ops that reference each other, now correctly
calculate their offset by adding up their own offset to the earlier
offsets in the tied operand chain. Not sure if that does/would come up
in a real case, but at least that's a sensible side effect.

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Add target-aware layout materialization

Dispatch-time data tiling assigns layouts inside dispatches, so the
phases before dispatch creation cannot see or propagate them.
Materializing the layouts during global optimization makes that phase
target aware on purpose: layouts propagate through the surrounding
tensor graph, and the packed contractions still fuse with their
epilogues and result unpacks.

Add the experimental --iree-opt-experimental-early-data-tiling flag. It
takes precedence over the other data-tiling placement flags, so
conflicting data-tiling flags are not an error when it is set, and the
route uses the operation families and encoding strategy of
dispatch-time data tiling.

The route applies to modules with a single llvm-cpu target on x86_64 or
AArch64 that uses the CPU encoding resolver without inner-tiled layouts,
and only with the default encoding strategy. For these modules, global
optimization propagates reshapes, normalizes contraction dimensions,
assigns and propagates encodings, and materializes them on the host. It
then records the target on the module, even if nothing was data-tiled.
Dispatch creation therefore skips encoding assignment for the whole
module, always fuses data-tiled ops with their epilogues and result
unpacks, and keeps the loop order of data-tiled convolutions. Other
modules keep dispatch-time data tiling. The enable_inner_tiled check
moves from the CPU encoding models to the Codegen utilities, so that the
eligibility check can share it.

On an Apple M3 Max (local-task, f32, median of 10), the route is within
noise of dispatch-time data tiling for a matmul with bias and ReLU, a
batch matmul with ReLU and a convolution with ReLU. x86_64 has not been
measured.

The layout decision is split over several passes, supports one CPU
target per module, and adds HAL and Codegen dependencies to the global
phases. The TODOs describe moving it into its own component that decides
per affinity.

name: clang-tidy

commit_message:
[DispatchCreation] Preserve the target of materialized tensor layouts

Once tensor layouts have been materialized for a device, dispatch
creation must neither assign encodings to them again nor compile them
for another device. Assigning encodings again re-encodes data-tiled
convolutions when convolutions are data-tiled, and tile shapes chosen
for one CPU can be unsupported or slow on another.

Record the target in a module attribute. Skip dispatch-time encoding
assignment for such modules, and reject them at the start of dispatch
creation when they are compiled for a different target, for several
targets, or for none. Modules without the attribute keep the existing
assignment, now wrapped in a module pass so that no function pass has
to read the attribute. Its options carry the operation families and
encoding strategy, so that printed pipelines and crash reproducers keep
them.

Nothing sets the attribute yet. A follow-up sets it in an experimental
route that materializes layouts during global optimization.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
name: clang-tidy

commit_message:
[DispatchCreation] Preserve the target of materialized tensor layouts

Once tensor layouts have been materialized for a device, dispatch
creation must neither assign encodings to them again nor compile them
for another device. Assigning encodings again re-encodes data-tiled
convolutions when convolutions are data-tiled, and tile shapes chosen
for one CPU can be unsupported or slow on another.

Record the target in a module attribute. Skip dispatch-time encoding
assignment for such modules, and reject them at the start of dispatch
creation when they are compiled for a different target, for several
targets, or for none. Modules without the attribute keep the existing
assignment, now wrapped in a module pass so that no function pass has
to read the attribute. Its options carry the operation families and
encoding strategy, so that printed pipelines and crash reproducers keep
them.

Nothing sets the attribute yet. A follow-up sets it in an experimental
route that materializes layouts during global optimization.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
name: setup / setup

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Add target-aware layout materialization

Dispatch-time data tiling assigns layouts inside dispatches, so the
phases before dispatch creation cannot see or propagate them.
Materializing the layouts during global optimization makes that phase
target aware on purpose: layouts propagate through the surrounding
tensor graph, and the packed contractions still fuse with their
epilogues and result unpacks.

Add the experimental --iree-opt-experimental-early-data-tiling flag. It
takes precedence over the other data-tiling placement flags, so
conflicting data-tiling flags are not an error when it is set, and the
route uses the operation families and encoding strategy of
dispatch-time data tiling.

The route applies to modules with a single llvm-cpu target on x86_64 or
AArch64 that uses the CPU encoding resolver without inner-tiled layouts,
and only with the default encoding strategy. For these modules, global
optimization propagates reshapes, normalizes contraction dimensions,
assigns and propagates encodings, and materializes them on the host. It
then records the target on the module, even if nothing was data-tiled.
Dispatch creation therefore skips encoding assignment for the whole
module, always fuses data-tiled ops with their epilogues and result
unpacks, and keeps the loop order of data-tiled convolutions. Other
modules keep dispatch-time data tiling. The enable_inner_tiled check
moves from the CPU encoding models to the Codegen utilities, so that the
eligibility check can share it.

On an Apple M3 Max (local-task, f32, median of 10), the route is within
noise of dispatch-time data tiling for a matmul with bias and ReLU, a
batch matmul with ReLU and a convolution with ReLU. x86_64 has not been
measured.

The layout decision is split over several passes, supports one CPU
target per module, and adds HAL and Codegen dependencies to the global
phases. The TODOs describe moving it into its own component that decides
per affinity.

commit_message:
[DispatchCreation] Preserve the target of materialized tensor layouts

Once tensor layouts have been materialized for a device, dispatch
creation must neither assign encodings to them again nor compile them
for another device. Assigning encodings again re-encodes data-tiled
convolutions when convolutions are data-tiled, and tile shapes chosen
for one CPU can be unsupported or slow on another.

Record the target in a module attribute. Skip dispatch-time encoding
assignment for such modules, and reject them at the start of dispatch
creation when they are compiled for a different target, for several
targets, or for none. Modules without the attribute keep the existing
assignment, now wrapped in a module pass so that no function pass has
to read the attribute. Its options carry the operation families and
encoding strategy, so that printed pipelines and crash reproducers keep
them.

Nothing sets the attribute yet. A follow-up sets it in an experimental
route that materializes layouts during global optimization.

targets, or for none. Modules without the attribute keep the existing

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Add target-aware layout materialization

Dispatch-time data tiling assigns layouts inside dispatches, so the
phases before dispatch creation cannot see or propagate them.
Materializing the layouts during global optimization makes that phase
target aware on purpose: layouts propagate through the surrounding
tensor graph, and the packed contractions still fuse with their
epilogues and result unpacks.

Add the experimental --iree-opt-experimental-early-data-tiling flag. It
takes precedence over the other data-tiling placement flags, so
conflicting data-tiling flags are not an error when it is set, and the
route uses the operation families and encoding strategy of
dispatch-time data tiling.

The route applies to modules with a single llvm-cpu target on x86_64 or
AArch64 that uses the CPU encoding resolver without inner-tiled layouts,
and only with the default encoding strategy. For these modules, global
optimization propagates reshapes, normalizes contraction dimensions,
assigns and propagates encodings, and materializes them on the host. It
then records the target on the module, even if nothing was data-tiled.
Dispatch creation therefore skips encoding assignment for the whole
module, always fuses data-tiled ops with their epilogues and result
unpacks, and keeps the loop order of data-tiled convolutions. Other
modules keep dispatch-time data tiling. The enable_inner_tiled check
moves from the CPU encoding models to the Codegen utilities, so that the
eligibility check can share it.

On an Apple M3 Max (local-task, f32, median of 10), the route is within
noise of dispatch-time data tiling for a matmul with bias and ReLU, a
batch matmul with ReLU and a convolution with ReLU. x86_64 has not been
measured.

The layout decision is split over several passes, supports one CPU
target per module, and adds HAL and Codegen dependencies to the global
phases. The TODOs describe moving it into its own component that decides
per affinity.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
name: clang-tidy

commit_message:
[GlobalOptimization] Add target-aware layout materialization

Dispatch-time data tiling assigns layouts inside dispatches, so the
phases before dispatch creation cannot see or propagate them.
Materializing the layouts during global optimization makes that phase
target aware on purpose: layouts propagate through the surrounding
tensor graph, and the packed contractions still fuse with their
epilogues and result unpacks.

Add the experimental --iree-opt-experimental-early-data-tiling flag. It
takes precedence over the other data-tiling placement flags, so
conflicting data-tiling flags are not an error when it is set, and the
route uses the operation families and encoding strategy of
dispatch-time data tiling.

The route applies to modules with a single llvm-cpu target on x86_64 or
AArch64 that uses the CPU encoding resolver without inner-tiled layouts,
and only with the default encoding strategy. For these modules, global
optimization propagates reshapes, normalizes contraction dimensions,
assigns and propagates encodings, and materializes them on the host. It
then records the target on the module, even if nothing was data-tiled.
Dispatch creation therefore skips encoding assignment for the whole
module, always fuses data-tiled ops with their epilogues and result
unpacks, and keeps the loop order of data-tiled convolutions. Other
modules keep dispatch-time data tiling. The enable_inner_tiled check
moves from the CPU encoding models to the Codegen utilities, so that the
eligibility check can share it.

On an Apple M3 Max (local-task, f32, median of 10), the route is within
noise of dispatch-time data tiling for a matmul with bias and ReLU, a
batch matmul with ReLU and a convolution with ReLU. x86_64 has not been
measured.

The layout decision is split over several passes, supports one CPU
target per module, and adds HAL and Codegen dependencies to the global
phases. The TODOs describe moving it into its own component that decides
per affinity.

commit_message:
[DispatchCreation] Preserve the target of materialized tensor layouts

Once tensor layouts have been materialized for a device, dispatch
creation must neither assign encodings to them again nor compile them
for another device. Assigning encodings again re-encodes data-tiled
convolutions when convolutions are data-tiled, and tile shapes chosen
for one CPU can be unsupported or slow on another.

Record the target in a module attribute. Skip dispatch-time encoding
assignment for such modules, and reject them at the start of dispatch
creation when they are compiled for a different target, for several
targets, or for none. Modules without the attribute keep the existing
assignment, now wrapped in a module pass so that no function pass has
to read the attribute. Its options carry the operation families and
encoding strategy, so that printed pipelines and crash reproducers keep
them.

Nothing sets the attribute yet. A follow-up sets it in an experimental
route that materializes layouts during global optimization.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
name: Analyze (javascript)

commit_message:
[Util] Fix crash in MergeIndexSwitchPattern when second op yields outer values

When MergeIndexSwitchPattern merged two scf.index_switch ops, it looked
up the second op's yielded values with IRMapping::lookupOrNull. A value
that is defined above both switches (a function argument, or a constant
hoisted out of the cases by canonicalization) is not in the mapping, so
the merged scf.yield was created with a null operand and the compiler
crashed. The first op's yields already use lookupOrDefault.

Use lookupOrDefault for the second op's yields too: values cloned from
either region and the first op's results are still remapped, and values
defined outside are used as-is. Add a test with cases that yield only
outer values.

Signed-off-by: jonathansong <7958352+jonathansong@users.noreply.github.com>
Assisted-by: Claude Code
name: pr-greeter

commit_message:
[Util] Ensure scf.index_switch ops share the same selector before merging

MergeIndexSwitchPattern merged two adjacent scf.index_switch ops whose
case values matched, without checking that they switch on the same
value. The merged switch takes the first op's selector, so the second
op's cases were then selected by the wrong value.

Adjacent switches on different values occur, for example, when two
dispatches of executables with different variant conditions are
recorded next to each other: each selects its variant (and workgroup
count) with its own value. After the merge, a dispatch ran with the
other executable's variant selection and workgroup count, and computed
only part of its output.

Require equal selectors before merging, and add a negative test.

Signed-off-by: jonathansong <7958352+jonathansong@users.noreply.github.com>

commit_message:
[HAL] Add command buffer flush and invalidate operations (#24945)

This PR adds HAL and runtime plumbing for ordered command-buffer buffer
flush and invalidate operations.

It introduces:

* `hal.command_buffer.flush_buffer`
* `hal.command_buffer.invalidate_buffer`
* HAL-to-VM lowering and VM imports
* runtime command-buffer API and vtable hooks
* VM module/shim plumbing
* inline command-buffer support
* deferred command-buffer recording/replay support
* HAL IR and HAL-to-VM test coverage

The operations carry a buffer reference, offset, and length and are
intended to represent execution-ordered cache maintenance for shared
non-coherent memory.

Stream-to-HAL lowering is intentionally left unchanged in this PR. Some
backends, especially Vulkan, require queue/submission-level handling to
preserve execution-time ordering because a HAL command buffer is
currently replayed into a single native `VkCommandBuffer`. Enabling
Stream lowering before that backend support exists could cause
unsupported runtime paths.

This PR therefore focuses on establishing the HAL/runtime infrastructure
first. Backend-specific execution support and Stream lowering can follow
separately.

Related to #24930.

commit_message:
[HAL] Add command buffer flush and invalidate operations (#24945)

This PR adds HAL and runtime plumbing for ordered command-buffer buffer
flush and invalidate operations.

It introduces:

* `hal.command_buffer.flush_buffer`
* `hal.command_buffer.invalidate_buffer`
* HAL-to-VM lowering and VM imports
* runtime command-buffer API and vtable hooks
* VM module/shim plumbing
* inline command-buffer support
* deferred command-buffer recording/replay support
* HAL IR and HAL-to-VM test coverage

The operations carry a buffer reference, offset, and length and are
intended to represent execution-ordered cache maintenance for shared
non-coherent memory.

Stream-to-HAL lowering is intentionally left unchanged in this PR. Some
backends, especially Vulkan, require queue/submission-level handling to
preserve execution-time ordering because a HAL command buffer is
currently replayed into a single native `VkCommandBuffer`. Enabling
Stream lowering before that backend support exists could cause
unsupported runtime paths.

This PR therefore focuses on establishing the HAL/runtime infrastructure
first. Backend-specific execution support and Stream lowering can follow
separately.

Related to #24930.

commit_message:
[Stream] Always map aliases to resolved resource ranges of the source op (#25026)

This ensures that all operands in the tied operand chain for a resource
will get mapped to the correct buffer range.

Previously, if the resource's buffer received a new allocation,
`stream.resource.subview` aliases (by nature of a byte subview, tied to
a different memory range) would still receive resource ranges relatively
to the old resource.
Additionally, all aliases of a given source would be processed from the
"nearest" subview in the alias chain. With multiple subviews in the same
tied operand chain, the offsets weren't computed relative to one
another.

Addressing the first problem enables the most practical use case.
SplitParameterEncoding in "consolidate" mode may need to place an
unmodified input weight into the output buffers, which means the weight
may end up in a packed allocation together with a pre-initialized output
parameter. To later fetch that input weight for dynamic initialization,
an explicit `subview` op is generated (*). Hoisting the constant out of
the execution scope establishes the new resource range, and the subview
should compute its resource range against that. Instead, the old
subrange would get used that was relative to the original SSA source
bound for deletion.
See `Stream/Transforms/test/schedule_allocation_subviews_constant.mlir`
for illustration.

(*) Whether that should be happening is a different matter. Accessing
the packed weight through `stream.async.slice` would've been preferable,
as per a [TODO in
SplitParameterEncoder](https://github.com/iree-org/iree/blob/0df50f9a8e40ab1878479124b952f45d9f8c0650/compiler/src/iree/compiler/Dialect/Stream/Transforms/SplitParameterEncoder.cpp#L1971).
Generally, we should let ScheduleAllocation operate on that abstraction
where a copy will implicitly be generated on writing to the range,
rather than have it account for explicit aliases in that of
`resource.subview`. For now I've preferred not to go into that
direction, because that switch requires larger-scale testing, and
currently explicit subview ops are expected to be supported in the input
IR to the allocator.

By implementing alias mapping as a DFS worklist and simply ignoring
values that have already been resolved to a resource range, nested
subviews, a.k.a. subview ops that reference each other, now correctly
calculate their offset by adding up their own offset to the earlier
offsets in the tied operand chain. Not sure if that does/would come up
in a real case, but at least that's a sensible side effect.

commit_message:
[Torch] Convert PT2E per-token quantization to LinalgExt

Convert quantized_decomposed.quantize_per_token and dequantize_per_token
to iree_linalg_ext.quantize_affine and dequantize_affine. As in torchao's
PerToken granularity, the block size is one along every input dimension
but the last, which each block spans, so the parameters are indexed by
the leading dimensions and the data path needs no reshape. The unit last
dimension that PT2E keeps in the parameters is dropped like any other
static unit dimension.

Per-token shares its operand checks with per-channel-group, which expect
one scale and zero point per block along each input dimension.

Quantize scales are widened as for the other granularities, so
quantization computes in the wider of the input and scale types, as the
per-token reference does, but in at least f32. Dequantization matches
the PT2E reference. The per-token reference adds the zero point before
rounding, so quantize ties with odd zero points differ from it and from
the Torch-to-Linalg lowering, which follows it.

Depends on the torch-mlir ops from llvm/torch-mlir#4765.

Signed-off-by: Roberto Laudani <laudani@roofline.ai>
name: runtime :: windows-2022

[Torch] Convert PT2E per-token quantization to LinalgExt

Convert quantized_decomposed.quantize_per_token and dequantize_per_token
to iree_linalg_ext.quantize_affine and dequantize_affine. As in torchao's
PerToken granularity, the block size is one along every input dimension
but the last, which each block spans, so the parameters are indexed by
the leading dimensions and the data path needs no reshape. The unit last
dimension that PT2E keeps in the parameters is dropped like any other
static unit dimension.

Per-token shares its operand checks with per-channel-group, which expect
one scale and zero point per block along each input dimension.

Quantize scales are widened as for the other granularities, so
quantization computes in the wider of the input and scale types, as the
per-token reference does, but in at least f32. Dequantization matches
the PT2E reference. The per-token reference adds the zero point before
rounding, so quantize ties with odd zero points differ from it and from
the Torch-to-Linalg lowering, which follows it.

Depends on the torch-mlir ops from llvm/torch-mlir#4765.

Signed-off-by: Roberto Laudani <laudani@roofline.ai>
name: Test TensorFlow
